Disadvantages to credit: even with small claims track, legal representation costs can be prohibitive for lower-income claimants; enforcement of civil judgments is not guaranteed — a claimant who wins a damages award still has to pursue the defendant to collect; complex civil cases in the High Court are very expensive and slow; the balance of probabilities standard means a claimant can win a civil case even when there is significant uncertainty about what happened.

practice_questions.text:
"The criminal justice system is more important than the civil justice system because it deals with harm to society as a whole, whereas civil law only protects individual interests."

Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should consider arguments that support this view, arguments that challenge it, and reach a substantiated conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10–12 marks): Full two-sided argument with named examples on each side. Engages with the claim about 'harm to society vs individual interests' and questions or refines it. Reaches a substantiated conclusion that goes beyond 'both are important'.

Secure (7–9 marks): Both sides developed with at least one named real-world example. Concludes with a partially substantiated judgement.

Developing (4–6 marks): Relevant arguments on both sides but limited development OR one-sided.

Emerging (1–3 marks): Basic points; little real-world example; largely descriptive.

Arguments supporting the statement: criminal law addresses acts (violence, theft, fraud) that threaten public safety and social order; criminal sanctions (imprisonment) have a deterrence effect that protects society; crime victims include not just the immediate victim but the wider community who feel less safe; the state's role in prosecuting crime reflects that these harms go beyond individual disputes.

Arguments challenging the statement: civil law also protects society-wide interests — employment law, consumer protection and environmental law benefit vast numbers of people, not just individuals; civil remedies for discrimination (e.g. under the Equality Act 2010) have changed workplace culture across entire industries; civil law regulates business conduct and economic life, which affects everyone; without civil law, harmful conduct that falls short of criminality would go unchecked; access to civil justice is a human right (Article 6 ECHR applies to both criminal and civil proceedings); tribunals such as employment tribunals have improved working conditions for millions.

Conclusion to credit: a judgement that goes beyond 'both are equally important' to identify which system has a stronger claim to primacy and why, with reference to named legislation or institutions. Strong answers may challenge the premise by arguing the boundary between the two systems is not fixed — Parliament can make certain civil wrongs criminal (e.g. health and safety breaches) and vice versa.

before.exam_tip_html: The criminal/civil distinction is tested frequently in short-answer and extended-response questions. The most common errors are: (1) using the wrong terminology — calling the person who brings a civil case the “prosecutor” when the correct term is “claimant”; (2) stating that both criminal and civil cases use “beyond reasonable doubt” — civil cases use the lower “balance of probabilities” standard; (3) failing to link the standard of proof to its justification — examiners reward answers that explain why criminal cases use a higher standard (the consequences of a wrongful conviction include imprisonment). For 8-mark Analyse questions, you will usually be asked to analyse advantages and disadvantages of one system, or to compare the two. Always name a specific court (magistrates’ court, Crown Court, County Court, employment tribunal) or a specific outcome (damages, injunction, imprisonment) to demonstrate precise knowledge and reach the higher bands.

practice_questions.text:
Which voting system is used to elect Members of Parliament to the House of Commons at a UK general election?
A) Single Transferable Vote
B) Additional Member System
C) First Past the Post
D) Proportional Representation List
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for C) First Past the Post.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by First Past the Post.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks: 1 mark for stating that the candidate with the most votes in a constituency wins the seat; 1 mark for adding that no majority is needed — a plurality is sufficient. A one-word answer scores 0.

practice_questions.text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of the First Past the Post voting system.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for identifying an advantage (e.g. produces clear majority governments); 1 mark for developing the advantage with a cause-and-consequence link (e.g. because the winning party typically secures enough seats to govern alone, it can implement its manifesto without coalition compromise); 1 mark for identifying a disadvantage (e.g. many votes are wasted in safe seats and smaller parties can win few seats despite significant national support); 1 mark for developing the disadvantage with a consequence (e.g. this reduces proportionality and may reduce voter turnout in constituencies where the result seems predetermined).

practice_questions.text:
Read the extract below and answer the question that follows.

"A non-partisan polling organisation surveyed 3,000 UK adults after the most recent general election. It found that 58% of respondents felt their vote had ‘made no real difference’ to the outcome, and 43% said they had voted for a party that won no seats in their constituency. The organisation concluded that under the current voting system, a significant proportion of voters feel disengaged from the electoral process."

Using the extract and your own knowledge, interpret what this source suggests about the relationship between voting systems and voter engagement.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for identifying the key finding (majority feel their vote made no difference; many voted for losing candidates); 1 mark for interpreting what this shows (under FPTP, votes for losing candidates in each constituency do not contribute to seat allocation, leading to ‘wasted votes’); 1 mark for using own knowledge (e.g. proportional systems such as AMS or STV are designed to reduce wasted votes and give smaller parties fairer representation, potentially improving engagement); 1 mark for a substantiated judgement (e.g. the source supports the argument that FPTP contributes to voter disengagement, though the survey question about ‘feeling your vote matters’ is subjective and other factors such as candidate quality or campaign style also influence engagement).

practice_questions.text: Analyse the extent to which First Past the Post serves the needs of UK democracy better than proportional representation systems.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Detailed two-sided analysis comparing FPTP and at least one named PR system (e.g. AMS for Scottish Parliament, STV for Northern Ireland). Named real-world anchors used on both sides (e.g. 2011 AV referendum result, devolved elections under AMS). Substantiated judgement explicitly weighs the criteria (stability vs proportionality) and reaches a clear conclusion.

Secure: Two-sided analysis with at least one named system or real reference. Both sides developed with at least one reason. Judgement present but may not be fully substantiated.

Developing: Relevant points but mainly one-sided, or both sides listed without development. Limited or no named real-world example.

Emerging: Basic points about FPTP or PR. Descriptive rather than analytical. No named system, no substantiated judgement.

practice_questions.text:
"The First Past the Post voting system should be replaced with a proportional representation system for Westminster elections."

Evaluate this statement. In your answer, consider arguments in support and arguments against, and reach a substantiated overall conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support: PR systems (such as AMS and STV, used in devolved elections) produce results more closely matching vote shares, reducing ‘wasted votes’. Smaller parties and minority views gain seats, giving a wider range of voters representation. Research on devolved elections suggests voters in Scotland and Wales find multi-party politics more engaging. Coalition governments can represent a broader range of voters’ priorities.

Arguments against: FPTP typically produces majority governments with a clear mandate, avoiding the instability and post-election negotiations typical of coalition politics. The 2011 UK referendum rejected changing to AV (a related system) by 67.9% to 32.1%, suggesting voters, at that time, preferred the existing system. The direct constituency MP link — where every voter can identify their own representative — is weakened by multi-member PR constituencies. Majority governments under FPTP can implement manifesto commitments without being blocked by coalition partners.

Mastering: Balanced evaluation with named real-world examples on both sides (e.g. AMS elections to Scottish Parliament, 2011 AV referendum, FPTP producing 1997 or 2019 landslide majorities). Conclusion that goes beyond ‘both have advantages’ and makes a substantiated judgement about which criteria for judging a voting system matter most.

Secure: Two-sided argument with at least one named system or real reference. Conclusion present but may not fully justify the weighing.

Developing: Relevant points, mainly one-sided or lacking named examples. Conclusion thin.

Emerging: Basic points, largely descriptive. No named example, no substantiated conclusion.

before.exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark Analyse or a 12-mark Evaluate question on voting systems, the most common error is to treat the answer as a list of pros and cons without making an explicit comparison or reaching a clear judgement. Examiners want you to weigh the arguments — for example: “FPTP produces stable majority governments, but at the cost of proportionality. The 2011 AV referendum showed that voters, at least at that time, preferred stability over greater proportionality. However, supporters of PR argue that fairness of representation matters more than ease of government formation.” Always name a real-world anchor: name a specific system (AMS, STV), name a specific election it is used for, or reference the 2011 referendum. A conclusion that merely says “both systems have advantages and disadvantages” without a judgement will not access the top band.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a reserved power that remains with the Westminster Parliament rather than devolved administrations?
A) Health policy in Scotland
B) Education in Wales
C) Immigration and nationality
D) Housing in Northern Ireland
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for C) Immigration and nationality.

practice_questions.text: Identify two services provided by local councils in the UK.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two distinct services from: waste collection; social care; housing; road maintenance; planning permission; parks and leisure facilities; libraries. Two very similar answers (e.g. “collecting rubbish” and “clearing waste”) score only 1 mark.

practice_questions.text: Describe what devolution means and how it has changed the governance of the UK.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for defining devolution (transfer of powers from Westminster to regional or national legislatures); 1 mark for a developed description (e.g. following referendums in 1997, the Scottish Parliament and Welsh Assembly were established in 1999 with powers over health, education and housing); 1 mark for a further feature (e.g. Westminster retains reserved powers including defence, foreign affairs and immigration); 1 mark for a further developed point (e.g. the Northern Ireland Assembly operates under a power-sharing arrangement following the Good Friday Agreement 1998). Evaluation not required.

practice_questions.text:
Read the extract below and answer the question that follows.

"A survey of 1,200 residents across four English cities, conducted by a civic research organisation in 2024, found that 67% of respondents could not name any service provided by their local council, and 78% did not know the name of their local councillor. The organisation suggested this ‘civic visibility gap’ was a barrier to holding local government to account."

Using the extract and your own knowledge, what does this source suggest about accountability in local government?
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for identifying the key finding (most residents cannot name local services or their councillor); 1 mark for interpreting what this shows (citizens cannot hold councillors accountable if they do not know what their council does or who represents them); 1 mark for using own knowledge (e.g. councillors are directly elected to represent wards and should be held accountable at local elections; low civic awareness reduces this accountability mechanism); 1 mark for a substantiated judgement (e.g. the source suggests civic education about local government is needed to make accountability meaningful, though the survey of four cities may not represent all areas of England, and awareness levels may be higher in areas with significant recent local controversies).

practice_questions.text:
A cross-party group of MPs is debating whether England should have its own devolved parliament, similar to the Scottish Parliament.

Discuss whether England should have a devolved parliament to address the imbalance created by the current devolution settlement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear two-sided discussion using named examples on each side (e.g. Scottish Parliament 1999, EVEL debate, West Lothian Question, English regional mayor models). Contrasting viewpoints connected with evaluative language. Substantiated judgement that weighs the arguments.

Secure: Two-sided discussion with at least one named example. Generally accurate. At least one viewpoint developed with reasoning.

Developing: Relevant points but mainly one-sided or without development. Limited or no named example.

Emerging: Basic points about devolution or Parliament. Descriptive rather than analytical. No named example or judgement.

practice_questions.text:
"Devolution has strengthened democracy in the UK by bringing power closer to citizens."

Evaluate this statement. In your answer, consider arguments in support and arguments against, and reach a substantiated overall conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support: Devolution has enabled Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland to make policy choices that reflect their own needs and priorities (e.g. Scotland’s approach to university tuition fees and free personal care). Democratic engagement in devolved elections has in some areas been higher than for Westminster. Bringing decisions closer to communities increases the relevance and responsiveness of government. The Good Friday Agreement, which underpinned the Northern Ireland Assembly, was essential to the peace process.

Arguments against: Devolution has created inconsistency: citizens in different parts of the UK receive different levels of public services depending on where they live, raising questions about fairness. The EVEL debate shows that devolution creates unresolved constitutional tensions at Westminster. England has no devolved parliament, meaning most English governance remains entirely centralised at Westminster. Critics argue devolution has fuelled rather than settled separatist sentiment, particularly in Scotland, where independence remains a major political question.

Mastering: Balanced evaluation with named real-world examples on both sides (e.g. Scottish Parliament, Northern Ireland Assembly, Good Friday Agreement, EVEL debate). Conclusion that goes beyond “it depends” and makes a substantiated judgement about whether, on balance, devolution has strengthened UK democracy.

Secure: Two-sided argument with at least one named example. Conclusion present but may not fully justify the weighing.

Developing: Relevant points, mainly one-sided or lacking named examples. Conclusion thin.

Emerging: Basic points, largely descriptive. No named example, no substantiated conclusion.

before.exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark Discuss question on devolution, avoid simply describing what devolution is — examiners want to see you weigh contrasting viewpoints. Present one view (e.g. devolution strengthens democracy by bringing decisions closer to communities) and then a contrasting one (e.g. devolution creates inconsistency and risks fragmenting the Union). Use a named example — reference the Scottish Parliament, the Senedd, or a specific policy difference between nations. For a 12-mark Evaluate, your conclusion must add genuine evaluative reasoning: decide which argument you find more convincing, supported by evidence. Watch out for the common error of confusing devolution with independence: state clearly that Westminster retains sovereignty, and that reserved powers (defence, foreign affairs, immigration) remain at Westminster level.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following courts handles the most serious criminal cases in England and Wales?
A) Magistrates' Court
B) County Court
C) Crown Court
D) Employment Tribunal
practice_questions.marks: C) Crown Court [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify two roles carried out by a judge during a Crown Court trial.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for each of two clearly distinct roles from the following:
- Managing the trial fairly and ruling on points of law
- Directing the jury on the legal standard they must apply (beyond reasonable doubt)
- Deciding the sentence if a guilty verdict is returned
- Advising on points of law (in Magistrates' Court context)
Do not credit two versions of the same role. Maximum 2 marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Magistrates' Court in England and Wales.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks: 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for development).
- Magistrates are lay (unqualified) volunteers from the community who are trained and supported by a legal adviser (1 + 1).
- The Magistrates' Court handles summary (less serious) criminal offences and can impose fines, community orders and short custodial sentences of up to six months (1 + 1).
- Around 95% of all criminal cases in England and Wales are heard in the Magistrates' Court (1 + 1).
Do not credit evaluation or comparison — description only.

practice_questions.text:
Read the extract and answer the question that follows.

A fictional broadsheet newspaper reported: 'A 2024 survey of 1,500 adults found that 62% believed ordinary people on juries are better placed than professional judges to decide questions of guilt, because they represent the public. However, 28% disagreed, arguing that jurors lack the legal knowledge to evaluate complex evidence fairly, while 10% were undecided.'

Using the extract and your own knowledge, explain what the extract tells us about public attitudes towards jury trials.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks: identification (1), interpretation (1), own knowledge (1), substantiated judgement (1).
- 1 mark for identifying what the source shows: a majority (62%) favour jury trial because they see juries as representative of the public.
- 1 mark for interpreting a key detail: nearly three in ten (28%) are sceptical, suggesting significant minority concern about jurors' legal competence.
- 1 mark for connecting to own knowledge: juries in England and Wales consist of twelve randomly selected registered voters aged 18-75 who must decide guilt to a criminal standard of beyond reasonable doubt.
- 1 mark for a substantiated judgement: the source suggests majority public support for jury trials exists, but the level of disagreement (28%) indicates debate about whether lay decision-making produces consistent, legally informed verdicts.

practice_questions.text: Analyse whether the use of lay magistrates to decide criminal cases is an effective way of delivering justice.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Balanced two-sided analysis with at least one named real-world example on each side (e.g. 95% of cases handled by magistrates, Magistrates' Court sentencing powers, criticisms of inconsistency or high conviction rates). A substantiated judgement that weighs the two sides and reaches a clear conclusion about overall effectiveness.

Secure (5-6 marks): Most points present, generally accurate, two-sided in places. At least one named example. A concluding judgement present but not fully developed.

Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant points but limited development, or one-sided argument. Some reference to courts or sentencing but no named specific example. Little or no weighing of evidence.

Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points about magistrates or courts; descriptive rather than analytical; no real-world example or judgement.

practice_questions.text: A local justice campaign group is calling for all criminal cases in England and Wales, including summary offences, to be decided by a judge alone rather than by lay magistrates or juries. Evaluate whether removing lay decision-makers from criminal courts would improve or damage justice in England and Wales.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12 marks): Full two-sided argument. Arguments for removing lay decision-makers (e.g. legal expertise, consistency, efficiency, reduced risk of jury bias) weighed against arguments for retaining them (democratic participation, community representation, public confidence, the principle that citizens are judged by peers, the Magistrates' Court's capacity handling 95% of cases). At least one named real-world example or institution on each side. A substantiated overall judgement in the conclusion that goes beyond 'it depends' and provides criteria for the judgement.

Secure (7-9 marks): Both sides covered, at least one named example, a judgement present but not fully substantiated.

Developing (4-6 marks): Some coverage of both sides but limited development; limited or no named examples; judgement weak or missing.

Emerging (1-3 marks): Basic points; largely one-sided; no named examples; no evaluative conclusion.

practice_questions.text:
What is the minimum age to vote in a UK general election?
A) 16
B) 17
C) 18
D) 21
practice_questions.marks: C) 18 [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State one group of people who are NOT allowed to vote in a UK general election.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of the following: members of the House of Lords; a person serving a custodial prison sentence; a person who is not registered to vote. One clearly stated answer is sufficient — no further explanation is required.

practice_questions.text: Explain why low voter turnout can be a problem for democracy.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. A strong answer develops a point with cause and consequence. For example: a government elected on low turnout may lack a strong mandate (1 mark) because only a small proportion of the total population voted for it (1 mark), which means it cannot claim to represent the views of most citizens (1 mark), and this weakens its democratic authority when passing laws (1 mark). Answers that state a problem without development score 1–2. Two fully developed points of cause and consequence can score up to 4.

practice_questions.text:
Read the extract below and answer the question that follows.

A fictional polling organisation surveyed 1,500 registered voters after the 2024 general election. Their report found: 'Among non-voters, the most common reasons given were disillusionment with all political parties (34%), feeling that their vote would make no difference (28%), and difficulty getting to a polling station on a working day (19%). Only 11% said they were satisfied with the result and had therefore chosen not to vote.'

Using the extract and your own knowledge, what does this source suggest about ways to increase voter turnout?
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for identifying what the source shows (non-voters give disillusionment and powerlessness as the main reasons for not voting); 1 mark for interpreting the significance of this (making voting easier on a working day addresses only 19% of non-voters, so turnout measures must also tackle engagement); 1 mark for applying own knowledge (linking to proposals such as compulsory voting, online voting, or political education); 1 mark for a substantiated judgement that combines the source and own knowledge (e.g. the source implies that convenience reforms alone would not solve voter apathy since disillusionment is the primary cause — deeper engagement measures are needed).

practice_questions.text:
A student council is debating whether to recommend that the local council pilot online voting for its next parish election. A local civic organisation has said: 'Making it easier to vote will automatically increase democratic participation.'

Discuss whether making voting easier is the most effective way to increase voter turnout.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Presents a sustained, balanced discussion with developed points on both sides, uses connective language, names at least one specific real-world example (e.g. Australia's compulsory voting system, the 16+ voting age in Scotland, or online voting trials in Estonia), and reaches a clear overall assessment of which measures are most effective and why.

Secure: Covers both sides with some development, includes at least one named real-world example, and reaches a general conclusion, though the reasoning may not be fully sustained.

Developing: Makes relevant points but the discussion is mainly one-sided or lacks real-world examples. May list proposals without weighing their effectiveness.

Emerging: Offers basic points about voting or turnout with little development, no named example, and no comparative judgement about the measures.

practice_questions.text:
A local charity has published a report arguing that the voting age for all UK elections should be lowered to 16, in line with the rules for Scottish Parliament and Senedd elections.

Evaluate whether lowering the voting age to 16 is the best way to increase democratic participation among young people.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full two-sided argument with multiple developed points for and against; names at least one specific real-world example per side (e.g. 16+ voting in Scottish Parliament and Senedd elections, or international examples such as Austria's national elections); reaches a substantiated overall judgement that weighs the evidence and explains why one position is stronger.

Secure: Both sides presented with at least one named real-world example; a conclusion is reached, but the evaluative judgement may lack full justification.

Developing: Relevant points on both sides but limited development; argument may be mainly one-sided or examples are generic ('in some countries') rather than named.

Emerging: Basic points about voting age with little development; one-sided or descriptive; no real-world named example; no substantiated conclusion.

Content that could be credited — Arguments in favour: Scottish Parliament and Senedd already allow 16-year-olds to vote; some 16-year-olds can pay tax; 16-year-olds can vote in Scottish Parliament and Senedd elections; building civic habits early may create lifelong voters; gives young people a voice on issues that affect them such as education and climate policy. Arguments against: 16-year-olds may lack life experience to make fully informed political decisions; turnout among 18-24 year olds is already lower than older age groups, so extending the age may not improve participation; other factors such as compulsory voting or better civic education may be more effective; changing the law risks party-political manipulation of which age group is more likely to support particular parties.

before.exam_tip_html: On an 8-mark “Discuss” or 12-mark “Evaluate” question about voter turnout or voting age, a very common mistake is writing a one-sided answer that only lists reasons for or against a proposal. Examiners reward responses that present both viewpoints, use connective language (“however”, “on the other hand”) and name a specific real-world example — for instance, Australia’s compulsory voting system, or the lower voting age in Scottish Parliament elections. For a 12-mark “Evaluate”, you must reach a substantiated conclusion: weigh which side has stronger evidence and explain why you reached that judgement. “It depends” with no further reasoning will not access the highest mark band. For the 4-mark “Source Interpretation” question, do not just summarise the source — identify what it shows, link it to your own knowledge and reach a judgement about what it means for democracy.

practice_questions.text:
What is the age of criminal responsibility in Scotland following the 2019 reform?
A) 8 years old
B) 10 years old
C) 12 years old
D) 16 years old
practice_questions.marks: C) 12 years old [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the minimum age at which a person can vote in Scottish Parliament elections.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for stating the age (16). 1 mark for a qualifying statement that shows understanding, such as: this age applies to Scottish Parliament and Scottish local council elections; or noting that the voting age for UK general elections remains 18. A bare number without context scores 1 mark only.

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways in which Scotland's legal system differs from the legal system in England and Wales.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks: 2 marks per difference (1 for identification, 1 for development).
- Scotland's highest criminal court is the High Court of Justiciary; criminal cases cannot be appealed to the UK Supreme Court, unlike in England and Wales (1 + 1).
- Scotland uses a 'not proven' verdict in addition to guilty and not guilty, which results in acquittal; England and Wales only have guilty and not guilty (1 + 1).
- Scots law is rooted in a blend of Roman civil law and common law; the English system is based on common law alone (1 + 1).
- The age of criminal responsibility in Scotland is 12, compared with 10 in England and Wales (1 + 1).
Maximum 4 marks. Avoid crediting evaluation.

practice_questions.text:
Read the extract and answer the question that follows.

A fictional think tank published: 'A 2024 poll of 2,000 people aged 14-17 in England found that 54% supported lowering the voting age to 16 for all UK elections, citing the fact that 16-year-olds can already leave school, work and pay tax. However, 33% opposed the change, arguing that maturity and political understanding are not guaranteed at 16, and 13% were undecided.'

Using the extract and your own knowledge, interpret what the extract tells us about the debate over voting age in the UK.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks: identification (1), interpretation (1), own knowledge (1), substantiated judgement (1).
- 1 mark for identifying the key finding: a majority of young people surveyed (54%) support lowering the voting age to 16 for all UK elections.
- 1 mark for interpreting a specific detail: the 33% who oppose cite maturity as a criterion, suggesting the debate is partly about capacity rather than just rights.
- 1 mark for own knowledge: 16-year-olds can already vote in Scottish Parliament and Welsh Senedd elections, showing the change is not unprecedented; the UK general election threshold remains 18.
- 1 mark for a substantiated judgement: the source suggests that young people themselves broadly favour extension of the voting age, though significant minority opposition within the age group itself means the debate is not straightforward.

practice_questions.text: Analyse whether it is fair that the age of criminal responsibility differs between England and Wales and Scotland.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Balanced two-sided analysis with named real-world examples on each side (e.g. Age of Criminal Responsibility (Scotland) Act 2019 raising the threshold from 8 to 12; England and Wales retaining 10; UN Committee on the Rights of the Child recommending at least 14 as an international standard). A substantiated judgement that weighs the two sides clearly.

Secure (5-6 marks): Both sides present, mostly accurate, at least one named example. A judgement present but not fully substantiated.

Developing (3-4 marks): Some coverage of both sides or one side well-developed; limited named examples; judgement weak or absent.

Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points; largely descriptive; no named examples; no judgement.

practice_questions.text: A parliamentary committee is reviewing whether the UK should adopt a single unified legal system to replace the current arrangement of three separate systems. Evaluate whether the UK would benefit from a single unified legal system.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12 marks): Full two-sided argument. Arguments for unification (consistency, efficiency, clarity for citizens moving between nations, reduced complexity) weighed against arguments for retaining separate systems (reflects distinct national identities and histories, Scotland's legal tradition pre-dates the Union, devolution respects democratic mandates, Scots law's 'not proven' verdict as a valued protection for defendants). At least one named example on each side. Substantiated overall judgement in the conclusion.

Secure (7-9 marks): Both sides covered, at least one named example, judgement present but not fully developed.

Developing (4-6 marks): Some coverage of both sides; limited named examples; judgement weak or missing.

Emerging (1-3 marks): Basic points; one-sided; no named examples; no evaluative conclusion.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is a tax on the income a person earns from employment?
A) Corporation tax
B) Council tax
C) Income tax
D) Value Added Tax
practice_questions.marks: C) Income tax [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify two services that are funded by local government.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each clearly distinct service, up to 2 marks. Acceptable answers include: waste collection; local road maintenance; social care for the elderly or disabled; planning and housing services; early-years or children's services. Two versions of the same service (e.g. 'bins' and 'recycling') score only 1 mark.

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways in which the UK government raises money through taxation.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 2 marks per described way (1 for naming the tax, 1 for describing what it is charged on or how it works). Example: income tax is charged on a person's earnings above the personal allowance (1 mark for naming income tax, 1 mark for describing it as a tax on earnings above a threshold). VAT is charged at 20% on most goods and services when sold (1 for naming VAT, 1 for describing it as a tax on the sale of goods and services). Other valid taxes include National Insurance and corporation tax. Avoid awarding the second mark for vague descriptions such as 'it is paid by everyone'.

practice_questions.text:
Read the extract below and answer the question that follows.

A fictional national newspaper published the following extract after the government's annual Budget:

'The Chancellor announced a £3.2 billion increase in NHS funding, to be funded partly by a 2p rise in the basic rate of income tax. Speaking after the statement, the leader of a national taxpayer campaign group said: “This is the right investment — a healthy population is a productive population and the NHS is under enormous pressure.” A spokesperson for a small business organisation responded: “Raising income tax reduces disposable income for workers and increases the pressure on businesses that top up employee pay. There must be a better way to fund the NHS.”'

Using the extract and your own knowledge, what does this source suggest about the challenges of funding public services?
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for identifying what the source shows (a tax rise to fund the NHS creates both supporters and critics); 1 mark for interpreting the significance (the extract reveals that funding decisions involve trade-offs between service provision and economic burden on taxpayers); 1 mark for applying own knowledge (linking to the general challenge of balancing public need — such as the NHS being the largest area of government spending — with tax burdens and national debt); 1 mark for a substantiated judgement combining source and own knowledge (e.g. the source illustrates that there is no politically neutral way to fund public services: both the decision to raise taxes and the decision not to have visible costs and consequences).

practice_questions.text:
A national charity has published a report claiming that cuts to social care funding leave vulnerable elderly people without adequate support.

Discuss whether the government should always prioritise health and social care when deciding how to spend public money.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained, balanced discussion presenting both sides with developed points, connective language, at least one named real-world example (e.g. the NHS, the social care funding gap, or the annual Budget process), and a clear overall assessment of which arguments are strongest.

Secure: Both sides covered with some development and at least one named real-world example. A conclusion is reached, though the evaluative judgement may not be fully sustained.

Developing: Relevant points made but mainly one-sided or lacking real-world examples. May list arguments without weighing them.

Emerging: Basic points about spending or health with little development, no named example, and no comparative judgement.

practice_questions.text:
A local pressure group is campaigning for the government to increase income tax to pay for better local social care services for elderly people, arguing that the current funding system is failing those most in need.

Evaluate whether raising income tax is the best way to fund improvements to public services such as social care.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full two-sided argument with multiple developed points for and against; names at least one specific real-world example per side (e.g. the NHS funded through National Insurance and income tax, the social care funding gap, VAT as an alternative revenue source, or international models such as social care insurance systems); reaches a substantiated overall judgement that weighs the evidence.

Secure: Both sides presented with at least one named real-world example; a conclusion is reached, but the evaluative judgement may lack full justification.

Developing: Relevant points on both sides but limited development; argument may be mainly one-sided or examples are vague.

Emerging: Basic points about tax or spending with little development; no named real-world example; no substantiated conclusion.

Content that could be credited — Arguments in favour: income tax is directly linked to ability to pay (higher earners pay more); it already funds the NHS and could similarly fund social care; raising it ensures a reliable income stream for services. Arguments against: raising income tax reduces disposable income and may reduce work incentives; VAT or corporation tax increases could raise equivalent revenue; alternative models such as insurance-based social care (as in Germany) spread cost differently; increasing borrowing or public-private partnerships may be more politically viable.

before.exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark “Discuss” or 12-mark “Evaluate” question on government spending, the most common mistake is writing a one-sided answer that either supports high public spending or criticises it without presenting the opposing view. Examiners reward answers that use connective language (“however”, “on the other hand”) and name a specific real-world example — for instance, the creation of the NHS, debates about welfare reform, or the distinction between health and social care funding. For a 4-mark “Describe” question, avoid drifting into evaluation; give two clearly described features and develop each one. For source-interpretation questions, do not simply list what the source says — reach a judgement about what it reveals and link it to your own knowledge of taxation or spending priorities.

practice_questions.text:
In which year was Magna Carta sealed?
A) 1066
B) 1215
C) 1689
D) 1998
Identify two rights protected by the Human Rights Act 1998.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for each of two clearly distinct rights, such as:
- The right to life
- The right to a fair trial
- Freedom from torture and inhumane treatment
- Freedom of expression
- The right to respect for private and family life
- Freedom of thought, conscience and religion
Do not credit two versions of the same right. Maximum 2 marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways in which trade unions have contributed to the development of workers' rights in the UK.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks: 2 marks per way (1 for identification, 1 for development).
- Collective bargaining: trade unions negotiate with employers on behalf of workers to secure better pay, conditions and rights, giving individual workers more power than they would have alone (1 + 1).
- Campaigning for legislation: union pressure contributed to Acts establishing paid holidays, sick pay, maternity and paternity leave, and the national minimum wage (introduced 1998) (1 + 1).
- Legal representation: trade unions advise and support members who face unfair dismissal or unsafe working conditions (1 + 1).
Avoid crediting evaluation. Description only.

practice_questions.text:
Read the extract and answer the question that follows.

A fictional campaign organisation published: 'A 2024 survey of 1,200 UK adults found that 71% agreed the Human Rights Act 1998 is an important protection of citizens' rights in the UK, while 18% thought Parliament should be able to override Human Rights Act rights if the national interest requires it, and 11% had no view.'

Using the extract and your own knowledge, explain what the extract tells us about public attitudes towards the Human Rights Act.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks: identification (1), interpretation (1), own knowledge (1), substantiated judgement (1).
- 1 mark for identifying the key finding: a large majority (71%) support the Human Rights Act as an important protection.
- 1 mark for interpreting a specific detail: 18% believe Parliament should be able to override it, suggesting a significant minority sees parliamentary sovereignty as more important than Convention rights.
- 1 mark for own knowledge: the Human Rights Act 1998 incorporated ECHR rights into domestic law; debate about whether Parliament should be able to override it reflects the tension between parliamentary sovereignty and human rights protection.
- 1 mark for a substantiated judgement: the source suggests strong majority public support for the Act, but the minority view highlights an ongoing democratic debate about the balance between elected parliamentary authority and rights protected by international treaties.

practice_questions.text: Analyse whether the Human Rights Act 1998 has been effective in protecting citizens' rights in the UK.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Balanced two-sided analysis with named real-world examples on each side (e.g. the Act allowing rights to be enforced in UK courts rather than Strasbourg; specific ECHR-based rights such as the right to a fair trial; criticisms that the Act is used to protect those whose actions are harmful to others; the debate about parliamentary sovereignty). A substantiated judgement weighing the two sides.

Secure (5-6 marks): Both sides present, mostly accurate, at least one named example. Judgement present but not fully substantiated.

Developing (3-4 marks): Some coverage of both sides; limited named examples; judgement weak or absent.

Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points; largely one-sided or descriptive; no named examples; no judgement.

practice_questions.text: A parliamentary commission is debating whether citizens' rights in the UK have developed sufficiently since 1215, or whether there is still more progress to be made. Evaluate how far the development of rights in the UK since Magna Carta has been a success story.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12 marks): Full two-sided argument using specific examples spanning different periods and rights areas. Arguments that the development has been a success (Magna Carta establishing rule of law, the Bill of Rights 1689 establishing parliamentary sovereignty, Representation of the People Acts extending the franchise, Equality Act 2010 protecting nine characteristics, Human Rights Act 1998, trade union rights). Arguments identifying ongoing gaps or contested issues (inequality in how rights are applied in practice, debate over the Human Rights Act's scope, trade union restrictions, ongoing campaigning organisations highlighting shortfalls). At least one named Act or campaign on each side. Substantiated overall judgement in the conclusion.

Secure (7-9 marks): Both sides covered with at least one named example; judgement present but not fully developed.

Developing (4-6 marks): Some coverage of both sides; limited named examples; judgement weak or missing.

Emerging (1-3 marks): Basic points about one or two Acts; one-sided; no evaluative conclusion.

practice_questions.text:
The legislature of the United States is called:
A) The Senate
B) Parliament
C) Congress
D) The Cabinet
practice_questions.marks: C) Congress [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify two ways in which citizens in a democratic system can participate in politics that citizens in a non-democratic system typically cannot.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each clearly distinct way, up to 2 marks. Acceptable answers include: voting in free and fair competitive elections; forming or joining opposition political parties; accessing independent media; protesting or demonstrating freely; criticising the government in public without fear of prosecution. Two versions of the same point (e.g. 'vote' and 'go to the polls') score only 1 mark.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the political system in the United States of America.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 2 marks per feature (1 for identifying the feature, 1 for developing it). Example: the USA uses a federal system of government (1 mark), meaning power is divided between a national federal government and fifty individual state governments (1 mark). The USA has a bicameral legislature called Congress (1 mark), consisting of two chambers: the Senate and the House of Representatives (1 mark). Other valid features include the separately elected President, the Bill of Rights, or the independent Supreme Court. Answers must describe rather than evaluate.

practice_questions.text:
Read the extract below and answer the question that follows.

A fictional international affairs research centre published the following findings in a 2024 briefing:

‘In a survey of 3,200 adults across twelve countries, 71% of respondents in established democratic states said they felt able to criticise their government without fear of personal consequences. In states classified as non-democratic by Freedom House, this figure fell to 18%. Of those in non-democratic states who said they felt unable to speak out, 64% identified fear of legal consequences as the primary barrier.’

Using the extract and your own knowledge, what does this source suggest about the difference between democratic and non-democratic political systems?
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for identifying what the source shows (a stark difference in citizens' freedom to criticise government between democratic and non-democratic states); 1 mark for interpreting the significance (the 18% figure in non-democratic states suggests political freedom is severely curtailed and that legal consequences deter participation); 1 mark for applying own knowledge (linking to features of non-democratic systems such as China's restrictions on free speech, press censorship, or the absence of multi-party elections); 1 mark for a substantiated judgement combining source and own knowledge (e.g. the source suggests that the absence of free speech fundamentally undermines accountability, because if citizens cannot criticise government without fear, governments cannot be effectively held to account).

practice_questions.text: Analyse the key differences between a democratic and a non-democratic political system, using one example of each type of system.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained analysis that breaks down the comparison into specific features (elections, civil liberties, rule of law, accountability, freedom of press), names at least one concrete example from each system (e.g. the USA's Bill of Rights or Congress vs China's single-party governance or press restrictions), weighs evidence on both sides, and reaches a substantiated judgement about which features are most important for democratic accountability.

Secure: Covers both democratic and non-democratic features with some development and at least one named real-world example from each system. A judgement is reached, though the analysis may not be fully sustained.

Developing: Relevant points about both systems but limited development; may list features without analysing them or name only one system specifically.

Emerging: Basic description of democracy vs non-democracy with little development; no named real-world examples; no analytical judgement.

practice_questions.text:
A school citizenship debate is considering the motion: ‘Democratic systems are always better for citizens than non-democratic ones.’

Evaluate this statement, referring to one democratic and one non-democratic political system outside the UK.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full two-sided argument with multiple developed points for and against the motion; names at least one specific real-world example per side (e.g. the USA's Bill of Rights, Congress, and Electoral College debates on the democratic side; China's single-party governance, restrictions on free speech, and economic development argument on the non-democratic side); reaches a substantiated overall judgement that weighs the evidence and explains why one position is stronger.

Secure: Both sides presented with at least one named real-world example; a conclusion is reached, but the evaluative judgement may lack full justification.

Developing: Relevant points on both sides but limited development; argument may be mainly one-sided; examples may be vague ('some democratic countries').

Emerging: Basic points about democracy with little development; no named real-world examples from outside the UK; no substantiated conclusion.

Content that could be credited — Arguments in support: free elections allow citizens to remove governments they disagree with; an independent judiciary protects individual rights; freedom of the press ensures accountability; the USA's Bill of Rights is a model of constitutionally protected rights. Arguments against: democratic systems can fail to protect minorities or reduce inequality; some non-democratic governments claim to command genuine popular support; China's government points to economic development and stability as benefits; different historical and cultural contexts mean democracy may not function the same way in every society.

before.exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark “Analyse” or 12-mark “Evaluate” question on how other countries are governed, a very common mistake is writing a vague comparison that does not name either country specifically or describe their actual features. Examiners reward answers that name the specific country, describe two or three concrete features of its system, and compare those features to the UK or to a contrasting system. Avoid value judgements that read as politically biased: write “critics argue that” or “supporters of this system contend that” rather than asserting one system is simply better. For the 12-mark Evaluate, you must reach a substantiated judgement — weigh the evidence and explain your conclusion. Simply listing facts about two countries without evaluation does not access the highest marks.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the age of criminal responsibility in England and Wales?
A) Eight years old
B) Ten years old
C) Twelve years old
D) Fourteen years old
practice_questions.marks: B) Ten years old [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify two types of crime.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each clearly distinct crime type, up to 2 marks. Acceptable answers include: violent crime; property crime; white-collar crime; organised crime; hate crime; cybercrime. Two versions of the same type (e.g. theft and burglary both described as property crime) score only 1 mark.

practice_questions.text: Describe two purposes of sentencing.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 2 marks per purpose (1 mark for naming the purpose, 1 mark for a developed description of what it means in practice). Acceptable purposes: retribution (punishment proportionate to harm caused); deterrence (discouraging the offender and others from future offending); public protection (removing the offender from society to prevent further harm); rehabilitation (changing the offender's behaviour through education or treatment); reparation (the offender making amends to victims or the community). Answers that only name the purpose without description score 1 mark each.

practice_questions.text:
Read the extract below and answer the question that follows.

"A report by the fictional Thornton Policy Institute (2024) examined reoffending data for 3,200 adults sentenced in England and Wales in 2021. It found that 49% of those given custodial sentences of under twelve months went on to commit a further offence within one year of release, compared with 28% of those given community orders with a supervision requirement. The report concluded that short prison sentences may be less effective at reducing reoffending than structured community-based alternatives for non-violent offenders."

Using the extract and your own knowledge, interpret what this source tells us about the effectiveness of different types of sentence.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for identifying what the source shows (higher reoffending rate among those given short custodial sentences compared to community orders); 1 mark for interpreting the significance (short prison sentences may not achieve the rehabilitation aim of sentencing as effectively as community orders); 1 mark for using own knowledge to develop the point (e.g. linking to the Criminal Justice Act 2003 aims of sentencing, the role of Youth Offending Teams, or research on factors behind reoffending); 1 mark for a substantiated judgement that goes beyond the source (e.g. noting that the source only covers non-violent offenders, or that public protection may still justify custody for violent offenders even where rehabilitation is less likely). Pure summary of the source without interpretation scores no more than 1 mark.

practice_questions.text: A local council is consulting on whether to invest more funding in youth offending prevention programmes or in additional police officers. Discuss whether prevention programmes are more effective than policing in reducing youth crime.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): A well-developed discussion presenting contrasting viewpoints with connectives (however, on the other hand). Both sides are developed with specific real-world examples — for example, the role of Youth Offending Teams (YOTs) in multi-agency prevention, or evidence that early intervention reduces reoffending; and the case for policing as deterrence or detection. A substantiated overall view is reached that weighs the evidence. Named examples are used (e.g. YOTs, community orders, the Criminal Justice Act 2003).

Secure (5-6 marks): Both viewpoints present and generally accurate. At least one named real-world example. The discussion uses some evaluative language but the conclusion may not be fully substantiated.

Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant points made but the answer may be one-sided or lack a named example. Some awareness of contrasting views but underdeveloped.

Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points about either prevention or policing. Little or no real-world reference. Descriptive rather than discursive.

practice_questions.text:
"Rehabilitation is the most important aim of sentencing."

Evaluate this statement with reference to different types of crime and sentence.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12 marks): A sustained two-sided evaluation. Arguments in support of rehabilitation as the priority aim: evidence that community sentences and treatment programmes reduce reoffending; the role of education and skills training in custody; the social cost of reoffending versus the cost of rehabilitation programmes. Arguments against: for serious violent or sexual offences, public protection and retribution may take precedence regardless of rehabilitation prospects; deterrence has value in signalling societal norms; some offenders may not be amenable to rehabilitation. Named examples used on both sides (e.g. Youth Offending Teams, community orders, custodial sentences for serious offences under the Criminal Justice Act 2003). Conclusion reaches a substantiated judgement — e.g. that the relative importance of each aim depends on the nature of the offence and the offender's circumstances, and that no single aim is appropriate for all situations.

Secure (7-9 marks): Both sides present, at least one named example. Conclusion present but may not be fully substantiated.

Developing (4-6 marks): Relevant points but largely one-sided or lacking named examples. Some awareness of counter-argument.

Emerging (1-3 marks): Basic listing of aims or types of sentence with little evaluation. No named examples or conclusions.

practice_questions.text:
The European Convention on Human Rights is enforced by which court?
A) The UK Supreme Court in London
B) The International Criminal Court in The Hague
C) The European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg
D) The UN International Court of Justice in New York
practice_questions.marks: C) The European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify two rights protected by the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each clearly distinct right, up to 2 marks. Acceptable answers include: the right to life; the right to education; the right to play; the right to protection from abuse and exploitation; the right to express views on matters affecting the child; the right to healthcare. Two variants of the same broad right score only 1 mark.

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways in which the Human Rights Act 1998 protects citizens in the UK.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 2 marks per way (1 mark for identifying the protection, 1 mark for a developed description). Acceptable points include: it allows citizens to challenge public authorities in UK courts without travelling to Strasbourg; public authorities including the police and NHS are legally required to act in accordance with Convention rights; courts must interpret legislation in a way that is compatible with Convention rights; Parliament must consider whether new legislation is compatible with Convention rights. A one-line statement without development scores 1 mark per point.

practice_questions.text:
Read the extract below and answer the question that follows.

"A fictional national charity, Rights Now UK, published a survey in 2024 showing that 61% of 16-18 year olds in its sample of 1,500 were unaware that the European Convention on Human Rights is separate from the European Union. The charity's director said: 'There is widespread confusion about what Brexit changed and what it did not. Many young people believe they lost ECHR protections when the UK left the EU. That belief is incorrect, and it matters, because citizens who don't know their rights are less able to exercise them.'"

Using the extract and your own knowledge, interpret what this source tells us about public understanding of human rights after Brexit.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for identifying what the source shows (widespread confusion among young people about whether Brexit removed ECHR protections); 1 mark for interpreting the significance (if citizens don't know their rights, they are less likely to enforce them — a practical barrier to human rights protection); 1 mark for using own knowledge to develop the point (e.g. explaining that the ECHR is a Council of Europe instrument, not an EU instrument, and that the Human Rights Act 1998 continues in domestic law); 1 mark for a substantiated judgement (e.g. the source highlights a civic education gap, or notes the limitation that the source relies on one charity's survey with a self-selected sample). Pure summary of the source without interpretation scores no more than 1 mark.

practice_questions.text: Analyse the view that international human rights agreements are effective at protecting people's rights.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): A well-developed two-sided analysis that weighs the strengths of international agreements (enforceable mechanisms such as the European Court of Human Rights, the Human Rights Act allowing domestic enforcement, ICC prosecution of war crimes, the monitoring role of the ICRC under the Geneva Conventions) against their limitations (reliance on state compliance, Security Council veto power, continued violations in signatory states, enforcement gaps). Both sides are supported with named real-world examples. A substantiated judgement weighs the evidence. Connectives used: however, on the other hand, in contrast.

Secure (5-6 marks): Both viewpoints present, at least one named example, generally accurate. Conclusion present but may not be fully substantiated.

Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant points on one or both sides but limited development. May list treaties without evaluating effectiveness. Some real-world reference.

Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points about a treaty or agreement with little analysis of effectiveness. No named examples or conclusions.

practice_questions.text:
"The Human Rights Act 1998 is essential to protecting citizens' rights in the UK and should never be repealed or significantly reformed."

Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12 marks): Sustained two-sided evaluation. Arguments in support: the Act allows citizens to challenge public authorities in UK courts without costly Strasbourg proceedings; it has led to changes in policy in areas such as police conduct and prisoner voting; public authorities are legally required to act in accordance with Convention rights; removing it would risk leaving citizens without effective domestic remedies for rights violations. Arguments against: critics argue it gives courts too much power over elected Parliament (sovereignty of Parliament concern); some argue judgements have prioritised offenders' rights over public safety; it could in principle be replaced by a domestic Bill of Rights that better reflects UK values; Parliament could still scrutinise legislation under any alternative framework. Named examples used on both sides. Conclusion reaches a substantiated judgement — e.g. whether the Act’s benefits of accessible domestic enforcement outweigh concerns about judicial power depends on how one balances parliamentary sovereignty against individual rights protection, and that judgement is itself a contested political question.

Secure (7-9 marks): Both sides present, at least one named example, conclusion present but may not be fully substantiated.

Developing (4-6 marks): Relevant points but largely one-sided or lacking named examples.

Emerging (1-3 marks): Basic description of the Human Rights Act with little evaluation.

practice_questions.text:
An e-petition on the UK Government website is automatically considered for a parliamentary debate when it reaches how many signatures?
A) 1,000
B) 10,000
C) 100,000
D) 1,000,000
Identify two ways citizens can bring about political change without standing for election.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each clearly distinct method, up to 2 marks. Acceptable answers: signing or organising a petition; lobbying an MP or councillor; joining or forming a pressure group; taking part in a lawful demonstration; campaigning on social media; writing to a newspaper; joining a trade union; volunteering in the community. Two versions of the same activity (e.g. 'sign a petition' and 'collect signatures for a petition') score only 1 mark.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between a pressure group and a political party.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. A strong answer develops the distinction with cause and consequence. For example: a pressure group campaigns to influence government policy on a specific issue (1 mark) without wanting to form a government itself (1 mark), whereas a political party contests elections in order to win power and govern the country (1 mark), fielding candidates at local and national elections with the aim of forming a government or opposition (1 mark). Answers that state the distinction without development score 1–2 marks. A single fully developed explanation with clear contrast can score 3–4.

practice_questions.text:
Read the extract below and answer the question that follows.

A fictional community campaigning organisation published the following account on its website in 2024:

‘For the past three years, residents of the Westbridge area have campaigned for safer road crossings near the primary school on Marsh Lane. We started with a paper petition of 400 signatures. We then used social media to reach 12,000 people and attracted local news coverage. Last month we met with our local councillor and our MP at a constituency surgery. The council has now agreed to install two new pedestrian crossings and a 20mph zone. The campaign has shown that organised local action, combining traditional and digital methods, can deliver real results.’

Using the extract and your own knowledge, what does this source suggest about how effective different methods of political participation can be?
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for identifying what the source shows (a combination of petition, social media and direct lobbying achieved a concrete local policy change); 1 mark for interpreting the significance (the source suggests that no single method is sufficient on its own — the combination of methods increased reach and direct access to decision-makers); 1 mark for applying own knowledge (linking to the range of participation methods available, such as the government e-petition system, constituency surgeries, or insider/outsider pressure group strategies); 1 mark for a substantiated judgement combining source and own knowledge (e.g. the source implies that local, tightly focused campaigns with a specific achievable goal are more likely to succeed than broad or vague campaigns, and that digital tools amplify but do not replace direct engagement with elected officials).

practice_questions.text:
A national student-led campaign is planning a demonstration outside Parliament to call for better mental health provision in schools. A civic education charity has argued: ‘Demonstration and protest are the most powerful tools available to citizens who want to bring about change.’

Discuss whether taking part in demonstrations and protests is the most effective way for citizens to bring about political change.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained, balanced discussion presenting both sides with developed points, connective language, at least one specific named real-world example (e.g. the Hillsborough families’ long campaign, the disability-rights campaigns leading to the Equality Act 2010, or the government e-petition system that secured debates on issues including animal welfare and veterans’ housing), and a clear overall assessment of which methods or combination of methods is most effective.

Secure: Both sides covered with some development and at least one named real-world example. A conclusion is reached, though the evaluative judgement may not be fully sustained.

Developing: Relevant points made but mainly one-sided or lacking real-world examples. May list methods without weighing their effectiveness.

Emerging: Basic points about protest or campaigning with little development, no named example, and no comparative judgement.

practice_questions.text:
A voluntary housing charity is considering how best to campaign for new government legislation to reduce homelessness. Its board is debating whether to operate as an insider group working directly with ministers, or as an outsider group running public campaigns and demonstrations.

Evaluate whether working directly with government as an insider group is more effective than campaigning publicly as an outsider group when citizens want to bring about political change.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full two-sided argument with multiple developed points for and against each approach; names at least one specific real-world example per side (e.g. the British Medical Association as an insider group regularly consulted on health policy; or the disability-rights campaign leading to the Equality Act 2010 as an example of sustained advocacy using a range of outsider and insider tactics); reaches a substantiated overall judgement that weighs the evidence and explains why one or the other approach, or a combination, is more effective.

Secure: Both sides presented with at least one named real-world example; a conclusion is reached, but the evaluative judgement may lack full justification.

Developing: Relevant points on both sides but limited development; argument may be mainly one-sided; examples may be generic ('some pressure groups') rather than named.

Emerging: Basic points about pressure groups or campaigning with little development; no named real-world example; no substantiated conclusion.

Content that could be credited — Arguments for insider group approach: direct access to ministers and civil servants allows policy influence before legislation is drafted; government is more likely to consult groups with recognised expertise; insider groups are perceived as moderate and responsible. Arguments for outsider group / public campaigning: can build mass public support that puts pressure on politicians at election time; does not require existing access or status; historical examples show public campaigns can shift opinion and eventually law; digital tools and social media amplify reach dramatically. Balance: the most effective campaigns often combine both — insider lobbying backed by demonstrated public pressure.

before.exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark “Discuss” question on how citizens bring about change, the most common error is simply listing methods without discussing how effective they are or presenting contrasting views. Examiners reward answers that use connective language (“however”, “on the other hand”), name a specific real-world example (the Hillsborough campaign, the Equality Act 2010, or the government e-petition system), and weigh the effectiveness of different approaches. For a 12-mark “Evaluate” question, you must reach a substantiated conclusion — for instance, arguing that the most effective method depends on the issue’s scale and the resources available to campaigners, and explaining your reasoning with evidence. For the 4-mark “Source Interpretation”, combine what the source says with your own knowledge and reach a judgement about what it shows — do not simply summarise the source.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the role of a magistrate?
A) A legally trained judge who presides over Crown Court trials
B) An unpaid citizen volunteer who decides cases in the magistrates' court
C) An elected official who sets local policing priorities
D) A citizen selected at random to decide the verdict in a Crown Court trial
practice_questions.marks: B) An unpaid citizen volunteer who decides cases in the magistrates' court [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State one difference between the role of a juror and the role of a magistrate.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks. A full statement of one clear difference scores 2 marks (1 mark for identifying the difference, 1 mark for development or accurate specificity). Acceptable differences include: jurors are selected randomly and serve in the Crown Court, whereas magistrates are volunteers who apply and are appointed to the magistrates' court; jurors decide the verdict in serious criminal trials, while magistrates hear and decide approximately 95% of criminal cases; jurors are guided by a judge on points of law, while magistrates are advised by a legally qualified court adviser. A vague or incomplete statement scores 1 mark.

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways in which citizens can take action to bring about change in the legal system.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 2 marks per way (1 mark for identifying the method, 1 mark for a developed description). Acceptable methods: joining or forming a pressure group to campaign for law reform; signing or organising a petition; lobbying MPs, councillors or government departments; participating in or organising a peaceful demonstration; using the media to publicise an injustice; bringing a legal challenge such as a judicial review; joining a trade union that campaigns for employment law reform. A one-line statement without development scores 1 mark per point.

practice_questions.text:
Read the extract below and answer the question that follows.

"A report by the fictional Centre for Civic Justice (2024) found that magistrates' courts in England and Wales dealt with 1.7 million criminal cases in 2023, compared with 93,000 Crown Court trials. The report noted that while magistrates are unpaid volunteers with no legal qualifications, their conviction rate for cases they hear is broadly comparable to that of Crown Court juries. The report argued that the magistracy represents a cost-effective way of delivering justice at scale, but warned that recruiting magistrates who reflect the diversity of local communities remains a significant challenge."

Using the extract and your own knowledge, interpret what this source tells us about the role of magistrates in the criminal justice system.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for identifying what the source shows (magistrates handle the vast majority of criminal cases — 1.7 million compared with 93,000 Crown Court trials); 1 mark for interpreting the significance (magistrates are central to the functioning of the criminal justice system at scale, not a minor supplement to professional judges); 1 mark for using own knowledge to develop the point (e.g. explaining the role of the court adviser in guiding magistrates on law, or the range of sentences available to magistrates compared to Crown Court judges); 1 mark for a substantiated judgement that goes beyond the source (e.g. noting the report's limitation — one organisation's data — or weighing the cost-effectiveness argument against the concern about diversity and the risk that a non-diverse bench may not reflect community perspectives). Pure summary scores no more than 1 mark.

practice_questions.text: A community group is considering which method of action to take to campaign for changes to sentencing law in their area. They are deciding between organising a petition and joining an established national pressure group. Discuss whether citizens working through established organisations are more effective at changing the law than taking individual or small-group action.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): A well-developed discussion with contrasting viewpoints, connectives and at least one named real-world example on each side. Arguments for collective/organisational action: established organisations (pressure groups, trade unions, charities) have professional staff, legal expertise, media contacts and sustained public profile that individual action cannot match; campaigns by Liberty (civil liberties), Amnesty International (human rights) or trade unions for employment law have achieved legislative change; the Hillsborough families campaign gained greater impact through collective sustained effort. Arguments for individual/small-group action: grassroots campaigns can set the agenda that larger organisations later adopt; petitions can quickly gather large numbers of signatories; social media has reduced the cost of organising without a formal structure; individual legal challenges (judicial review) have directly changed government policy. A substantiated overall view is reached.

Secure (5-6 marks): Both viewpoints present, at least one named example, generally accurate. Conclusion present but may lack full substantiation.

Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant points on one or both sides but limited development or no named example.

Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points about campaigning with little or no real-world reference.

practice_questions.text:
"The most important way citizens can participate in the legal system is by serving as jurors or magistrates rather than by campaigning to change the law."

Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12 marks): Sustained two-sided evaluation. Arguments in support: formal roles within the system (jury, magistrate, special constable, tribunal lay member) are constitutionally significant, with jurors deciding guilt or innocence in the most serious cases and magistrates handling approximately 95% of criminal cases; these roles ensure democratic participation in the delivery of justice; without citizens in these roles the system could not function. Arguments against: formal roles operate within existing law and cannot change it; campaigning for legal reform has a longer-term impact on the system itself — the Hillsborough families campaign led to changes in inquest law and police accountability; the Stephen Lawrence campaign led to the Macpherson Report and race relations law reform; trade union campaigning secured employment protections that shaped the law for millions of workers; in a democracy, the ability to change law may be more fundamental than administering existing law. Named examples used on both sides. Conclusion reaches a substantiated judgement — e.g. that formal roles are essential for day-to-day justice delivery while campaign action shapes what the law is; both matter, but their importance depends on whether the question is about administering the law as it stands or improving it.

Secure (7-9 marks): Both sides present, at least one named example, conclusion present.

Developing (4-6 marks): Relevant points but largely one-sided or lacking named examples.

Emerging (1-3 marks): Basic description of one or two roles with little evaluation.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following correctly describes the threshold for a UK e-petition to be considered for a parliamentary debate?
A) 1,000 signatures
